The distance between two points on a number line is the positive difference of their co-ordinates.
Co-ordinate of B is 2, co-ordinate of E is 5, and \(5 > 2\).
\(d(B, E) = 5 - 2 = 3\)

The distance between two points on a number line is the positive difference of their co-ordinates.
Co-ordinate of J is \(-2\), co-ordinate of A is 1, and \(1 > -2\).
\(d(J, A) = 1 - (-2) = 3\)

The distance between two points on a number line is the positive difference of their co-ordinates.
Co-ordinate of P is \(-4\), co-ordinate of C is 3, and \(3 > -4\).
\(d(P, C) = 3 - (-4) = 7\)

Co-ordinate of J is \(-2\), co-ordinate of H is \(-1\), and \(-1 > -2\).
\(d(J, H) = -1 - (-2) = 1\)

\(d(K, O) = 0 - (-3) = 3\)

\(d(P, J) = -2 - (-4) = 2\)

Co-ordinate of Q is \(-5\), co-ordinate of B is 2, and \(2 > -5\).
\(d(Q, B) = 2 - (-5) = 7\)

\(d(A, B)\) is the positive difference of the co-ordinates \(x\) and \(y\).
Here \(x = 1\), \(y = 7\) and \(7 > 1\).
\(d(A, B) = 7 - 1 = 6\)

Here \(x = 6\), \(y = -2\) and \(6 > -2\).

Here \(x = 4\), \(y = -8\) and \(4 > -8\).
\(d(A, B) = 4 - (-8) = 12\)

Of three collinear points, the one that lies between the other two is the point for which the two shorter distances add up to the longest one.
\(d(P, R) + d(R, Q) = 7 + 3 = 10 = d(P, Q)\)
So the points are collinear and R lies between P and Q, that is \(P-R-Q\).

Check whether any two of the distances add up to the third.
\(d(S, T) + d(R, T) = 6 + 4 = 10 
e 8\); \(d(R, S) + d(R, T) = 8 + 4 = 12 
e 6\); \(d(R, S) + d(S, T) = 8 + 6 = 14 
e 4\).
No sum of two distances equals the third, so the points R, S and T are not collinear.

Of three collinear points, the one that lies between the other two is the point for which the two shorter distances add up to the longest one.
\(d(A, C) + d(C, B) = 9 + 7 = 16 = d(A, B)\)
So the points are collinear and C lies between A and B, that is \(A-C-B\).

No sum of two distances equals the third, so the points L, M and N are not collinear.

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives X-Y-Z. That would require \(d(X,Y) + d(Y,Z) = d(X,Z)\), i.e. \(15 + 7 = 8\), which is false. The only sum that closes is \(d(X,Z) + d(Z,Y) = 8 + 7 = 15 = d(X,Y)\), so Z lies between X and Y and the correct betweenness is X-Z-Y.]

Of three collinear points, the one that lies between the other two is the point for which the two shorter distances add up to the longest one. Here the longest distance is \(d(X, Y) = 15\).
\(d(X, Z) + d(Z, Y) = 8 + 7 = 15 = d(X, Y)\)
So the points are collinear and Z lies between X and Y, that is \(X-Z-Y\).
_note: The book's answer key prints "X-Y-Z", which is wrong. \(X-Y-Z\) would require \(d(X,Y) + d(Y,Z) = d(X,Z)\), i.e. \(15 + 7 = 8\), which is false. The only sum that works is \(8 + 7 = 15\), so Z is the point in between and the correct betweenness is \(X-Z-Y\).

Two arrangements are possible on the number line.
Case 1: C lies between A and B, that is \(A-C-B\). Then \(d(A, B) = d(A, C) + d(C, B) = 10 + 8 = 18\).
Case 2: C does not lie between A and B, so A and B are on the same side of C, that is \(C-B-A\). Then \(d(A, B) = d(A, C) - d(C, B) = 10 - 8 = 2\).
\(d(A, B) = 18\) or \(d(A, B) = 2\)

X, Y and Z are collinear, so two arrangements are possible.
Case 1: Y lies between X and Z, that is \(X-Y-Z\). Then \(d(X, Z) = d(X, Y) + d(Y, Z) = 17 + 8 = 25\).
Case 2: Z lies between X and Y, that is \(X-Z-Y\). Then \(d(X, Z) = d(X, Y) - d(Y, Z) = 17 - 8 = 9\).
\(d(X, Z) = 25\) or \(d(X, Z) = 9\)

Draw a line and mark A, B, C on it in that order, so that B lies between A and C.
Since \(A-B-C\), \(l(AB) + l(BC) = l(AC)\).
\(l(AB) = l(AC) - l(BC) = 11 - 6.5 = 4.5\)

Draw a line and mark R, S, T on it in that order, so that S lies between R and T.
Since \(R-S-T\), \(l(RT) = l(RS) + l(ST)\).
\(l(RT) = 2.5 + 3.7 = 6.2\)

Draw a line and mark X, Y, Z on it in that order, so that Y lies between X and Z.
Since \(X-Y-Z\), \(l(XY) + l(YZ) = l(XZ)\).
\(l(YZ) = l(XZ) - l(XY) = 3\sqrt{7} - \sqrt{7} = 2\sqrt{7}\)

Three non-collinear points do not lie on one line, so joining them in pairs gives three segments that enclose a closed figure with three sides.
The figure formed is a triangle.
